Improvements in weather forecasting over recent decades have created large economic value by giving farmers better information at the moments when weather-sensitive decisions matter most. More accurate forecasts help farmers choose when to plant so seeds are not lost to unexpected frost, flooding, or drought conditions. They also support more precise irrigation decisions, allowing water to be applied when crops need it and avoided when rainfall is expected. Better forecasts help farmers time harvesting before damaging storms, excessive rain, or heat reduce crop quality and yield. By reducing avoidable crop losses and improving the use of labor, machinery, water, and other inputs, modern forecasting directly strengthens agricultural productivity and farm income.

More reliable and earlier warnings of severe storms also generate major economic and human benefits. When hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, blizzards, or dangerous thunderstorms are forecast with more lead time, communities can evacuate vulnerable areas, protect homes and businesses, move vehicles and equipment, close roads, reinforce infrastructure, and stage emergency personnel and supplies. These preparations reduce property damage by giving people and institutions time to secure assets before the storm arrives. They also reduce loss of life by allowing residents to leave dangerous areas, seek shelter, and avoid travel during the most hazardous conditions. The value of these warnings is especially large because severe weather can produce enormous losses in a short period, and even modest improvements in preparation can prevent substantial harm.

Weather forecasting has also improved efficiency across transportation and energy systems. Airlines use forecasts to plan safer and more fuel-efficient routes, avoid turbulence and storms, reduce delays, and manage airport operations more effectively. Shipping companies use marine forecasts to choose routes that avoid dangerous seas, high winds, and costly disruptions, protecting cargo while improving fuel use and scheduling reliability. Electricity grid operators rely on forecasts to anticipate heating and cooling demand, predict wind and solar generation, schedule backup power, and balance supply and demand in real time. These uses lower operating costs, reduce waste, improve reliability, and help large networks function more smoothly, showing that better forecasts deliver economic value far beyond the weather services themselves.
